abstract: Abstract Introduction Mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) can modulate immune responses and suppress inflammation in autoimmune diseases. Although their safety has been established in clinical trials, the efficacy of MSCs is inconsistent due to variability in potency among different preparations and limited specificity in targeting mechanisms driving autoimmune diseases. Methods We utilized high-dimensional design of experiments methodology to identify factor combinations that modulate gene expression by MSCs to mitigate inflammation. This led to a novel MSC-based cell therapy, HXB-319. Its anti-inflammatory properties were validated in vitro by flow cytometry, RT-PCR, and mass spectrophotometry. To evaluate in vivo efficacy, we treated a diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH) mouse model (C57Bl/6). Seven days post-DAH induction with pristane, mice received either MSCs or HXB-319 (2X10 6 cells, IP). On day 14, peritoneal lavage fluid (PLF) and lung tissue were collected for flow cytometry, histopathological examination, and mRNA. Results HXB-319 increased gene expression levels of anti-inflammatory, angiogenic, and anti-fibrotic factors (eg, TSG-6, VEGF, and HGF). KEGG pathway analysis confirmed significant activation of relevant anti-inflammatory, angiogenic, and anti-fibrotic proteins, corroborating RT-PCR results. In the DAH model, HXB-319 significantly reduced lung inflammation and alveolar hemorrhage compared to MSC-treated and untreated DAH mice. HXB-319 treatment also significantly decreased neutrophils, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and RORγT cells, increased FoxP3 + cells in PLF, and reversed alterations in mRNA encoding IL-6, IL-10, and TSG-6 in lung tissue compared to DAH mice. Conclusion HXB-319 effectively controls inflammation and prevents tissue damage in pristine-induced DAH, highlighting its therapeutic potential for autoimmune inflammatory diseases.

Materials and methods
Preparation of HXB-319 from healthy human MSCs
Healthy human donor bmMSCs (or MSCs in this manuscript), obtained using a good manufacturing process (GMP), were procured from the cell core at the Seidman Cancer Center at Case Western Reserve University (CWRU). All cell manipulations were performed using previously published protocols.
31
The cells were cultured through a maximum of 4 passages.
Preparation of HXB-319
We used a data-driven, high-dimensional-design of experiment
s
(HD-DoE)-based methodology
37
,
38
to identify and address complex microenvironment abnormalities of autoimmune diseases (ie, SLE). Using a quality by design (QbD) approach and a robotic platform, we explored 96 combinational conditions of 12 factors typically present in an inflammatory microenvironment of autoimmune disease over 6-36 hours and thereby determined the optimal combination of factors and duration of exposure. The expression levels of 52 genes, assessed by RT-PCR after RNA extraction, were analyzed using a predictive mathematical model (MODDE, DoE statical package)
37
to identify key therapeutic targets selected for their anti-inflammatory, anti-fibrotic, and angiogenic effects. Our training medium, tailored to selectively and potently promote the development of an anti-inflammatory phenotype that can modify autoimmune diseases (eg, AAV, anti-GBM disease, and SLE), is detailed in our patent application (PCT/US20/40931) (
Supplementary Data 4, Patent Application
).
Briefly, HXB-319 is produced by incubation (in a 5% CO
2
humidified atmosphere at 37 °C for 18 hours) of mesenchymal stromal cells at 85%-100% confluence in low glucose Dulbecco’s modified Eagles medium (DMEM) (Mediatech, Cat. #10-014-CM), enriched with a proprietary cocktail of factors optimized to induce anti-inflammatory characteristics which includes TNF-α, Type-I, and Type-II interferon stimulating factors (Patent pending,
Supplementary Data 6
). Next, the cells are harvested using standard protocols and frozen in 5% HSA in Plasmalyte-A with 5% DMSO.
HXB-319 characteristics and product identity
The Cellular Therapy Laboratory at CWRU determined the surface marker characteristics of cryopreserved bmMSCs and HXB-319 using the MacsQuant analyzer (Miltenyi Biotec). Human bmMSCs are identified by staining of ≥ 90% of the cells for surface markers CD105, CD73, and CD90, and by ≤5% positivity for hematopoietic markers CD45 and CD14 (all antibodies from Miltenyi Biotec.)
39
(
Supplementary Figure 1A
). Additionally, the differentiation and proliferation capacity of donor MSCs and HXB-319 were assessed with chondrogenic, and osteogenic differentiation assays (
Supplementary Figure 1C
), and direct cell counting (
Supplementary Figure 1D
) and viability (
Supplementary Data Table 3
). Light microscopic examination of HXB-319 as compared to their naïve bmMSC donor was not different from each other. There were no differences in cell morphology, adherence to the plastic, and cell viability differences during cell culture assays before and after a freeze-thaw cycle
39
using the CytoSmart instrument (Corning). The characteristics of HXB-319 have been identified further through gene expression analysis and by secretory product examination.
RNA isolation and RT-qPCR assays
At the final passage, bmMSCs or HXB-319 were plated into 12 well plates or T12.5 cm flasks and grown until 90%-95% confluent. Cells were washed with PBS and then cultured in either DMEM-LG serum-free medium (bmMSC) or in our proprietary induction medium (HXB-319) for 18 hours. After this incubation, cells were re-suspended, aliquots for cell count and viability assessment were taken, and then RNA was extracted from the residual cells using a commercial RNeasy Mini kit (Qiagen cat# 74106).
For quantitative real-time polymerase chain reactions (RT-qPCR), RNA was extracted from cultured cells or lung tissue using an RNeasy Mini kit, and cDNA was generated using a High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (Applied Biosystems, Thermo Fisher Scientific cat# 4368813) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Reactions were performed on the AB Real Time PCR 7400 Fast system using Applied Biosystems SYBR Green PCR Master Mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific cat# 4364346) (Primer list is provided in
Supplementary Appendix Table 1
).
Mass spectrometric secreted protein analysis
Secreted proteins from GMP-grade MSCs and HXB-319 cells from different donors were profiled using mass spectrometry (MS) in collaboration with the Proteomics Core Labs at CWRU using previously published methods.
40
Frozen HXB-319 and naïve bmMSCs from the same donor were thawed and incubated in serum-free media (DMEM) for 18 hours. Cell media was collected and analyzed for secreted proteins and compared, using 4 paired sets of GMP-grade HXB-319 cells and naïve bmMSCs from the same donors.
Protein pathway analysis was performed by proteomics core personnel blinded to the hypothesis and experimental arms using methods published previously.
40
A total of 1591 proteins are significantly different between the HXB-319 and naïve bmMSCs were identified and analyzed using 3 different protein pathway analysis software platforms (Crosstalker, Scaffold, and then Adventia, iPathway-KEGG analysis).
Animals
Female C57Bl/6 (6-8-week-old) mice were purchased from The Jackson Laboratories and housed in the AAALAC-International accredited ultra-barrier facility at Case Western Reserve University (CWRU). All experiments were conducted with an IACUC-approved protocol (2017-0144). To induce pulmonary hemorrhage (Zhuang, 2017 #8812), 40 mice at 10 weeks of age received a single intraperitoneal injection (IP) of 0.5 mL pristane (2,6,10,14-tetramethylpentadecane, Sigma P2870-100ML), whereas 15 others were given the same volume of sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Seven days after pristane injection, 18 mice (DAH group) were given IP 0.5 mL serum-free tissue culture medium, whereas others were given IP 2 × 10
6
of either HXB-319 (
n
= 10), or naive MSCs (
n
= 12) in 0.5 mL of fresh serum-free tissue culture medium.
Although mice were expected to survive longer,
41
many mice died or became severely clinically ill, prompting the termination of the experiment on day 14 following pristane induction. Whenever possible, tissue was recovered from mice that died spontaneously prior to the endpoint of the experiment. On day 14, all surviving mice were euthanized per the IACUC protocol. Blood (1.5 mL) and peritoneal lavage fluid samples were collected using previously published protocols.
12
After gross examination of the lungs, RNA was extracted from a portion using the RNeasy Mini kit (Qiagen cat# 74106) and the remaining lung tissue was fixed in 10% PBS buffered formalin. Fixed lung tissue was embedded in paraffin, sectioned at 4 μm, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) using standard techniques. Deparaffinized lung sections were also stained for neutrophils (Ly-6G/Ly6C Antibody, RB6-8C5) and monocytes/macrophages (F4/80/EMR2, Clone 521204) (each diluted at 1:100, both from Biotechne), and developed using the Vectastain Elite ABC-HRP Kit (Rat IgG), and Bloxall (both from Vector Labs), after quenching endogenous peroxidase, blocking Fc receptors using nonspecific antibody, and blocking endogenous biotin and avidin, all following the manufacturer’s instructions. Gross appearance and histologic sections of lungs stained by H&E and immunohistochemistry were examined by experienced pathologists (SNE & NPZ), blinded to experimental groups, to detect intra-alveolar hemorrhage and alveolar capillaritis, according to previously published criteria.
6
,
10
Secreted protein analysis
The kynurenine content in serum-free culture medium of HXB-319 or naïve MSC samples was quantified via an IDO Activity colorimetric kynurenine assay,
42
,
43
using L-kynurenine (Sigma cat# K8625) as standards. Optical density was read at 490 nm using a Perkin Elmer EnSpire 2300 Multilabel plate reader, and the mean kynurenine concentration in each sample was taken from interpolation to a kynurenine standard curve.
Mouse serum IL-1 beta ELISA
Mouse serum was tested for IL-1β using an IL-1β Sandwich ELISA Kit (Proteintech cat# KE10003) following the manufacturer’s protocol.
Flow cytometry
Cellular flow cytometric analysis in the peritoneal lavage fluid was performed as suggested
7
,
12
to analyze changes in the cellular content of the pristane-induced model, using previously published methods.

,
12
,
41
Suspensions of stained cells (antibodies, fluorophores, and sources are specified in
Supplementary Appendix Table 2
) were analyzed in a Becton Dickinson LSRFortessa instrument, using the collateral software from the instrument manufacturer.

sxae078_Suppl_Supplementary_Materials
body:
Significance statement
We have developed a novel and proprietary educated/primed MSC-based cell therapy (HXB-319) designed to secrete anti-inflammatory factors, growth factors, and chemokines that help to suppress inflammatory responses from immune cells, promote angiogenesis, and suppress major signaling pathways responsible for fibrosis preventing irreversible organ damage.
Introduction
Pulmonary capillaritis, seen in autoimmune diseases such as anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis (AAV) including microscopic polyangiitis and granulomatous polyangiitis, anti-basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE),
1
can lead to life-threatening diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH). Approximately 50% of patients who develop DAH die despite aggressive therapy with corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, cytotoxic agents, and plasmapheresis,
2-4
and survivors may face chronic lung damage and fibrosis. A more effective, but less toxic therapy for autoimmune-related DAH is needed.
Intraperitoneal injection of pristane in mice can induce a disease resembling SLE with varying degrees of glomerulonephritis, arthritis, and pulmonary hemorrhage, depending upon the mouse strain.
5
Abnormalities in innate, cellular, and humoral immunity lead to markedly elevated titers of autoantibodies and pro-inflammatory cytokines including type I IFN and, in turn, organ damage.
5-10
The heterogeneity in organ involvement and progression in the murine model is a reflection of the disease in the genetically diverse human population.
5
Pulmonary capillaritis, which is less frequent in humans, is restricted to the H-2b mouse strains (C57Bl/6 and C57Bl/10). Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) have a major role in the acute lung injury of DAH induced by pristane,
6
characterized by capillaritis, and alveolar hemorrhage histologically equivalent to the autoimmune DAH seen in humans.
6-11
Pulmonary hemorrhage develops approximately 2 weeks post-induction, whereas other organ involvement (eg, glomerulonephritis) may require months to develop.
12
Thus, the pristane mouse model offers insight into autoimmunity, aiding in the evaluation of experimental treatments for human disease.
10
Many studies, using both allogeneic and autologous human mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs), have demonstrated regulatory effects on immune cells in diverse autoimmune disease models and in human clinical trials,
13-36
but the MSCs’ immunoregulatory actions and efficacy are heavily dependent on the patient’s unique cytokine and inflammatory cellular environment, which can influence their therapeutic effects.
25-28
To overcome the challenges of the variability in MSCs’ therapeutic responses, we developed a proprietary culture media comprised of specific cytokines and factors that allow for the “training” of MSCs prior to therapeutic administration. Specifically, we developed trained allogeneic human bone marrow-derived (bm) MSCs (HXB-319) targets autoimmune diseases with abnormal type I IFN activation that present with severe autoimmune inflammation and vasculitis, leading to end-organ damage and hemorrhage as seen in the pristane-induced mouse model of lupus. Based on our results in vitro, HXB-319 regulates the function of a variety of cells (eg, neutrophils, lymphocytes, and dendritic cells) that underlie autoimmune disease, while also increasing Treg cells that control inflammation.
In this study, we delivered either naive MSCs or our trained HXB-319 cell therapy to treat pristane-induced DAH in C57Bl/6 mice at the onset of pulmonary hemorrhage.

Results
Phenotype of HXB-319 cells in vitro
Cell surface markers and cell viability were studied to analyze the properties of HXB-319 before and after a freeze/thaw (F/T) cycle. Preconditioned HXB-319 cells or plain MSCs exhibited >90% positivity for CD105, CD73, and CD90, and <5% positivity for CD45 and CD14 (See
Supplementary Figure 1A and B
), indicating both naïve MSCs and HXB-319 were still of mesenchymal cell lineage, consistent with minimal criteria for defining MSCs International Society for Cellular Therapy (ISCT) standards.
44
,
45
In 4 independent experiments, each with cells from a different donor, the viability and proliferative rate did not differ between MSC and HXB-319 cells after an F/T cycle, when compared to the same cultures assessed without freezing (
Supplementary Data 1, Table 3
). In independent and blinded technicians’ hands, there was no morphological difference between the HXB-319 and MSCs with respect to cellular adherence or colony duplication rate (
Supplementary Figure 1D
). Contact inhibition was observed in HXB-319 as well as in MSCs cultures. The differentiation assays performed showed that HXB-319 has the same osteogeneic and chondrogenic differentiation capabilities (
Supplementary Figure 1C
).
Indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO), a marker of anti-inflammatory potency for MSCs,
46
was measured by RT-PCR in cells from 3 adult donors and commercially available MSCs (Rooster Biosystems). Expression of IDO was dramatically (>50 000-fold) increased in HXB-319 cells compared to naïve MSCs (
n
= 4) (
Figure 1A
). HXB-319 cells (
n
= 4) also secreted 2.3 times more kynurenine (the IDO enzymatic product) into culture media compared to naive MSCs (
Figure 1B
).

P
< .001, Students

-test). (B) The IDO activity as measured by Kynurenine levels in the tissue culture media at 24 hours’ time point, demonstrated as fold difference as compared to the MSCs (

n
= 4) and HXB-319 (

P
< .05 for all figures (Student’s

Gene expression profiling of HXB-319
Compared to naive MSCs from the same donor, HXB-319 showed significant differences in the expression of multiple genes by quantitative RT-PCR analysis.
Notably, HXB-319 expressed significantly more anti-inflammatory genes (eg, TSG-6, 26-fold; CTLA-4, 3.4-fold; CD274/PD-L1, 17-fold; TLR-3, ~9-fold; AKT, 2.4-fold; iNOS, 4.9-fold; CX3CL1, 90-fold), while pro-inflammatory markers (eg, TLR-7, TLR-9) were significantly decreased compared to MSCs from same donor (
Figure 1C
and
1D
). Notably, TLR-7 and IL-23 are important contributors to inflammation, working with IL-17 to induce the differentiation of naïve CD4+ T cells into highly pathogenic helper T cells (Th17) that produce inflammatory cytokines such as IL-17 isoforms, IL-6, and TNF-α.
HXB-319 exhibited a 4.7-fold increase in CD146 gene expression; this marker indicates a commitment to vascular smooth muscle lineage, with perivascular features and significant anti-inflammatory properties (
Figure 1E
).
47-49
Moreover, HXB-319 displayed elevated gene expression of VEGF-A, known for its role in promoting vascularization and serving as a marker for regenerative potential (
Figure 1E
). Finally, HXB-319 expressed significantly more RNA encoding hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) and c-Met (the receptor for HGF), hallmarks of anti-fibrotic potential (
Figure 1F
).
Protein pathway analysis of secreted proteins
The secretome of HXB-319 cells significantly differed from that of naïve MSCs; we identified 1591 differentially expressed proteins by mass spectrometry in 4 sets of MSCs and paired HXB-319 cells from the same bone marrow donors. Analysis with Advantia Protein Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) Pathway Analysis software (Release 100.0+/11-12)
50
,
51
yielded 353 differentially expressed genes (of a total of 1247 measured genes) in 37 pathways that were significantly impacted. Concurrently, the Gene Ontology Consortium
52
criteria revealed 569 gene ontology terms, 3 miRNAs, 71 genes, and 120 chemical upstream regulators that were enriched. Both approaches converge on HXB-319 upregulation of anti-inflammatory, angiogenic, and antifibrotic pathways (
Figures 2
and
3
). Moreover, HXB-319 exhibited reduced pro-inflammatory proteins, modulated by activation of the IL1 receptor antagonist (IL-1RA, encoded by IL1RN), a natural inhibitor of pro-inflammatory IL-1β.
53
Figure 2.
Three major pathways were activated by HXB-319 (KEGG, Ipathway analysis). Anti-inflammatory and angiogenic signaling: IL-1RN (IL-1 receptor antagonist) activation that results in IL-1β, and control of IL-17 pathway by IK-βα, TSG-6, and potent angiogenic protein pathway upregulation.
Figure 3.
Anti-fibrotic signaling: MMP signaling activation, HGF/c-Met activation, INHBA (Inhibin A and Follistatin activation that suppress TGF-β). Red font/arrows are used for significantly upregulated, and blue font/arrows are used for significantly downregulated molecules.
In vivo potency of HXB-319 compared to MSCs
Many mice given pristane became very ill toward the end of the second week post-injection,
41
exhibiting poor feeding, weight loss (~10%), and difficulty mobilizing due to tachypnea. Despite the initial expectation of survival beyond 14 days, we terminated the experiment on day 14 post pristane injection due to apparent morbidity as required by our IACUC. After injection of pristane, sham-treated DAH mice had a survival rate of 80% (24/30), while MSC-treated mice had a 73.6% (14/19) (
P
> .05, not significant) survival rate (
Figure 6
). Thus, MSC treatment did not improve survival compared to DAH mice. In contrast, all HXB-319-treated mice survived until day 14 after pristane injection (14/14) and showed no clinical symptoms of breathing or feeding difficulty, and were able to maintain normal ambulation correlating to the gross and microscopic pathology.
Pulmonary pathology
Postmortem lung tissues from 4 groups of mice were studied: untreated healthy mice (C57Bl/6), pristane-injected mice (DAH), DAH mice followed by MSC (MSC) treatment, and DAH mice followed by HXB-319 treatment. Alveolar hemorrhage (
Figures 4
-
6
) differed significantly among the experimental groups (
χ
2
= 22.6,
P
< .001). Alveolar hemorrhage was evident grossly in 72.2% of mice in the DAH group, a rate significantly higher than either the control C57Bl/6 (0%) or HXB-319 (30%) groups (Fisher’s
P
< .001 and  = .039, respectively). HXB-319 mice did not differ significantly from the control C57Bl/6 (
P
= .15). In contrast, the MSC group (83.3%) did not differ significantly from DAH mice (
P
= .40) but was significantly higher than in C57Bl/6 (
P
< .001).
By microscopic examination, extravasated erythrocytes filled, and often distended 59.7 ± 9.3% of alveoli in mice with gross hemorrhage (
Figures 4
-
6
), irrespective of treatment group (
F
= 0.88,
P
= .43). Mice without gross hemorrhage, including all control C57Bl/6 and most HXB-319 mice, had no or rare (<5% of) alveoli containing any erythrocytes, and the extent of microscopic alveolar hemorrhage was highly and significantly correlated to gross lung hemorrhage (
r
= 0.97,
P
< .001). By immunohistochemistry, most infiltrating leukocytes were neutrophils. F
= 1.01,
P
= NS), but was significantly higher (
F
= 7.2,
P
< 0.02) in mice with alveolar hemorrhage (14.9 ± 2.3) than in mice without hemorrhage (5.94 ± 1.5). Monocytes/macrophages were detected in 20%-67.6% of mice given pristane; the density of monocytes/macrophages (overall 11.5 ± 1.8 cells per 40× field) did not vary by treatment group (

= 1.07,
P

P
< .05) in mice with alveolar hemorrhage (8.87 ± 2.6) than in mice without hemorrhage (0.25 ± 0.25).
Figure 4.
Images from mice representative of each experimental group. Grossly, the C57Bl/6 group had normal lungs that were pink and crepitant; microscopic examination of H&E revealed fully patent air spaces devoid of erythrocytes and delimited by thin walls (H&E) with no infiltration by leukocytes. The majority of mice in both the DAH and MSC groups had extensive hemorrhage: zones of deep red to black color and tactile induration grossly, large numbers of erythrocytes in alveolar walls alveoli (H&E), and infiltration of alveolar walls by prominent neutrophils (some indicated by red arrows) and less conspicuous monocytes/macrophages (some indicated by blue arrows). Most HXB-319 treated mice had no (grossly or microscopically) evident hemorrhage, but nearly all (88%) had neutrophils and sparse macrophages infiltrating alveolar walls (final microscopic magnification 50×).

Discussion
Short-term pre-incubation in our proprietary cytokine cocktail initiates a powerful anti-inflammatory response in mesenchymal stromal cells. As demonstrated by a matrix assay approach,
54
quantitative RNA analysis of gene expression, flow cytometric analysis of functionally relevant surface markers, protein-based assay of the secretome, and proteomic pathway analysis, HXB-319 are trained and highly charged mesenchymal stromal cells. HXB-319 secretes a network of potent interactive anti-inflammatory, regenerative (angiogenic), and anti-fibrotic factors. Importantly, HXB-319 cells express significantly increased levels of a wide panel of anti-inflammatory markers (see results),
55
,
56
compared to naive MSCs. In our hands, pristane-induced DAH in C57Bl/6 is similar to previous reports.
8
,
40
,
54
Treatment with HXB-319 statistically significantly improved survival and reduced many of the key metrics in pristane-induced DAH often to levels that do not differ significantly from untreated healthy C57Bl/6 mice. Conversely, treatment with naive MSCs typically did not result in significant differences from untreated DAH. Overall, treatment with HXB-319 is more effective than naíve MSCs in ameliorating end-organ damage in autoimmune disease.
Several mechanisms are implicated in the improved efficacy of HXB-319. Overexpression of TSG-6 by mesenchymal stromal cells has been shown to prevent lung injury in other models (eg, LPS-induced acute lung injury, a mode of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and silica-induced acute pulmonary inflammation). It is suggested that TSG-6 secreted by MSCs activates NF-κB, inhibits the NLRP3 inflammasome pathway in lung macrophages, and diminishes pulmonary neutrophil counts.
57-59
We report here that HXB-319 highly expressed TSG-6, and secreted TSG-6 significantly higher than MSCs and exerted potent effects on neutrophils, expression of pro-inflammatory markers (TLR-7, -9, and IL-23), and lung injury in vivo. In vitro HXB-319 highly expresses fractalkine (CX3CL1), known to powerfully influence leukocyte trafficking at the endothelium
25
and augment NK cell IFN-γ expression and secretion, and NK cytolytic function.
60
These characteristic effects of HXB-319 may play a role in controlling pulmonary inflammation and angiogenesis in DAH.
Human mesenchymal stromal cells polarize into distinct phenotypes following specific toll-like receptor (TLR)-activation.
61
TLR3-priming favors an immunosuppressive (MSC2) phenotype, expressing CCL-10, CCL-5, and to a lesser degree IL-4 and IL-10, while TLR4-priming triggers a pro-inflammatory phenotype (MSC1), secreting IL-6 and IL-8, and even reversing MSC-established suppressive effects.
61
Previous reports suggested improved outcomes of interferon-primed MSCs in the Graft vs Host Disease and acute radiation lung injury models. Clinical application of primed MSCs has not been established yet.
62
,
63
HXB-319 carries the characteristics of the MSC2 immunosuppressive pattern with TLR-3 overexpression. In contrast to naïve MSCs, the phenotypic and functional changes in HXB-319 cells are sustained sufficiently to allow these cells to exert salutary effects in vivo for 7 days. Infusion of HXB-319 into DAH mice reduced pulmonary hemorrhage by >50% compared to either mice left untreated or given naïve MSCs. Moreover, HXB-319 treatment prevented mortality in all mice tested, most likely due to the secretion of immunosuppressive and anti-inflammatory factors. Postmortem analysis of DAH mice treated with HXB-319 IP shifted the number, and the phenotypic distribution of intraperitoneal leukocytes from levels seen in diseased mice left untreated or given naïve MSCs, toward the level seen in normal mice. Overall, the secreted factors of our HXB-319 significantly reduce both alveolar hemorrhage and expression of inflammatory markers associated with alveolitis evoked by intraperitoneal injection of pristane into mice. Our data suggests that the mechanism of action of HXB-319 in this project has been through secreted factors released into the mouse circulatory system after intraperitoneal injection.
Alveolitis due to neutrophil activation in response to immune complexes is a component of several autoimmune diseases, including SLE, AAV, and anti-GBM disease. Disruption of the delicate alveolar capillaries by florid neutrophil margination and degranulation leads to extensive intra-alveolar damage and hemorrhage. This complication exhibits ~50% mortality. The available therapy is often toxic, with limited efficacy. Herein, we report that HXB-319 cell therapy ameliorate
s
the evolution of alveolar capillaritis and DAH, reduce
s
the expression of several proinflammatory cytokines in lung tissue and reduces the influx of immature inflammatory monocytes and neutrophils into the peritoneum. SLE is a prototype for autoimmune inflammatory disease that shares a pathogenesis with a variety of other autoimmune diseases that result in pulmonary or renal endothelial damage. DAH ensues in a variety of other systemic autoimmune inflammatory vasculitis disorders, including anti-GBM disease and AAV. Similar to SLE, in both anti-GBM disease and AAV, neutrophils and NETosis play an important role in vascular injury and damage resulting in alveolar hemorrhage and/or chronic glomerulosclerosis and end-stage kidney disease. SLE, anti-GBM disease, and AAV all have significant morbidity and mortality regardless of the standard of care (SOC) therapies used, which include corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, immunomodulators, and occasionally chemotherapy, plasmapheresis, or dialysis. There is a significant need for potent therapies like HXB-319 that are less toxic and less immunosuppressive than SOC. HXB-319 could potentially improve mortality and morbidity in those patients with end-organ damage that fail SOC. In mouse experiments, HXB-319 (2 × 10
6
cells/mouse) was well tolerated and safe, with no observed side effects. Furthermore, pre-clinical dosing and distribution studies are required before clinical trials can be planned.
Conclusion
Training of bone-marrow-derived mesenchymal stromal cells by incubation in media containing a key combination of cytokines and growth factors, established by a QbD approach that integrates the cellular response with mathematical modeling, significantly diminishes disease activity in a pristane-induced murine model. A single dose of HXB-319 prevented alveolar hemorrhage in vivo. While both HXB-319 and MSC treatments were well tolerated, naïve MSC treatment did not improve the survival rate of the DAH mice model, nor did it reduce alveolar hemorrhage. Immune licensing, priming, and stimulating mesenchymal stromal cells with cytokines or growth factors enhance their anti-inflammatory potency in vitro.
60-62
Our report demonstrates that MSCs can be guided to increase anti-inflammatory efficacy and acquire potent multilayered anti-fibrotic, and angiogenic effects.
As judged by ISCT consensus criteria (quantitative RNA analysis of selected gene(s); flow cytometry analysis of functionally relevant surface markers such as CD274 and protein-based secretome assay),
54
HXB-319 is a potent anti-inflammatory, anti-fibrotic, and angiogenic cell product. In addition, HXB-319 can alleviate capillaritis and alveolar hemorrhage, reduce the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines in lung tissue, and reduce the influx of immature inflammatory monocytes into the peritoneum, all features of pristane-induced DAH.
Further development of specifically trained mesenchymal stromal cells as a novel cell therapy platform may prove effective for the treatment of other autoimmune diseases, especially those characterized by autoimmune small vessel vasculitis and/or fibrosis.
